one_liner: Dart 3.13 AOT binary beats per-node malloc/free C by 1.17x on benchLANG binary trees; Dart source unpublished.
what_it_does: A row from benchLANG, a small Nix-pinned benchmark of 19 languages on five workloads; it is not a library. The binary-trees workload builds a depth-19 stretch tree, a depth-18 long-lived tree and 2^(22-d) short-lived trees at each even depth d from 4 to 18 (68,332,206 nodes in all, counted from the loop bounds in languages/C/bench.c), sums each with a recursive check and discards it; the C and C++ versions free every node inside the timer. The Dart row is a single bench.dart compiled by `dart compile exe` into a self-contained AOT executable, but that file is not in the repository, so its node layout, leaf representation and timing points cannot be read.
how_it_is_fast: The win comes from the memory manager rather than Dart code generation: the Dart VM allocates by bumping a pointer in a semi-space young generation (up to 16 MB per semi-space on 64-bit by default in SDK 3.13.0) and reclaims dead trees with a copying scavenge whose cost scales with survivors, while C pays one malloc and one free call per node plus a second traversal to free. Old-generation marking and sweeping run concurrently on helper threads by default (concurrent_mark and concurrent_sweep true, 2 marker tasks in 3.13.0's flag_list.h), so part of the reclamation is off the timed main thread; the README publishes no CPU time for this row. This mechanism is inferred from the VM defaults, since the Dart program itself could not be read.
when_to_use: You already ship Dart (Flutter back ends, CLI tools) and wonder whether a pass that builds many short-lived tree nodes (ASTs, parse trees, immutable persistent structures) needs to move to C through FFI: with default VM settings the AOT binary beat naive malloc/free C on this workload.
Allocation-heavy code whose objects die before the next young-generation scavenge, the case bump allocation and copying collection handle cheaply.

As one data point when picking a garbage-collected AOT language: Dart's 0.865 s ties OCaml (0.865 s), is close to Bun (0.816 s) and Nim (0.809 s), and is well ahead of Go (1.796 s) and Node (1.444 s) on this row of the same table.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Dart beats C in general: it lost the other four workloads and is 2.13x slower in total (20.754 s vs 9.762 s; Fibonacci 8.135 vs 1.694 s, strings 6.523 vs 2.132 s, primes 2.963 vs 2.725 s).
Against C or C++ that allocates tree nodes from an arena, pool or bump allocator: the benchmark's C uses malloc/free per node by design, and the advantage is the allocator, not compiled-code quality.

Memory- or size-constrained deployments: whole-process peak RSS was 74.6 MiB against 33.3 MiB for C, and the stripped executable 5617 KiB against 26 KiB, because the AOT binary embeds the Dart runtime.
When you need reproducible evidence: the Dart program is not published, the table is one run per language, and the raw results file with checksums and CPU times is not committed.

integration.form: source-drop (benchmark program; the Dart file itself is not published)
integration.dependencies: Dart SDK 3.13.0 from nixpkgs-unstable (flake.lock pinned); any pubspec or package use is not documented
integration.min_toolchain: Dart 3.13.0 as measured; `dart compile exe` has no optimisation-level option for native executables (in the SDK's compile command only the wasm target takes -O), so this is the default AOT pipeline
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux only (Arch Linux, Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz)
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable: a single-isolate workload (the VM's GC helper threads run alongside it)

gotchas: The Dart source is missing, so the row cannot be reproduced. .gitignore ignores every file and re-includes extensions language by language with no !*.dart rule, languages/ has no Dart directory, and raw languages/Dart/bench.dart returns 404, although run_benchmarks.sh changes into languages/Dart and runs `dart compile exe bench.dart`. A fresh clone fails at the Dart compile step. The algorithm, node layout and timer placement cannot be checked, and checksum agreement cannot be confirmed because benchmark_results_*.txt is not committed either.

Harness asymmetry, stated in the README ('native code frees inside the timer, GC runtimes collect when they like'): C and C++ walk every tree a second time to free each node inside the timed region, while a GC runtime just drops the root. With 16 MB semi-spaces and concurrent old-generation mark and sweep on helper threads, some reclamation happens off the main thread and some garbage may still be live at exit, so the row compares allocation strategies rather than languages.

Small single-run margin: 0.865 s against C's 1.010 s is 14% less time, but the native malloc rows running the same algorithm already spread from 0.986 s (Fortran) to 1.147 s (C++); against the best native row the margin is about 1.14x (derived from page data), from one run with no variance reported.

The README says `-S` 'strips the snapshot'; in the Dart SDK, -S is --save-debugging-info, which removes debugging information from the executable and saves it to bench.sym. That affects only the reported 5617 KiB binary size, not timing.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued benchLANG binary-trees rows Dart (0.865 s) ties OCaml, trails Java (0.347 s) and Bun (0.816 s), and beats C# (0.931 s); prefer the OCaml or C# rows when you need an inspectable program (their sources are committed), and LangArena's Java and Bun Binarytrees::Obj entries for stronger C++ baselines. Cite this row only when Dart is already your stack.
verified_claims_summary: benchLANG's 3 September 2026 run (one run per language, Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, Arch Linux) timed binary trees at 0.865 s for Dart 3.13.0 AOT (dart compile exe, default VM GC settings) against 1.010 s for C (gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops, malloc/free per node) and 1.147 s for C++ (g++ 16.2.0, new/delete). That is about 1.17x and 1.33x faster, or roughly 12.7 against 14.8 ns per node over 68.3 million nodes (derived from page data). The Dart program behind the number is not published.
status_note: Small single-author MIT repo (8 stars, last commit 2026-09-03) with Nix-pinned toolchains, but the Dart row cannot be reproduced from it because bench.dart was never committed; treat it as a first-party anecdote at tier C at most (a move to D is defensible if unpublished code counts as no valid measurement).
